newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Troubled regional Asian currencies recover poise.
newsitem.headline: Troubled regional Asian currencies recover poise.

text.p: Strife torn Southeast Asian currencies recovered some of their poise on Tuesday as operators decided it was time to bank some profits on the U.S. dollar's recent sharp rise.
Despite calmer and more stable conditions, dealers and economists were still jittery and said the risk to the downside still loomed large for most of the region's currencies.
The market is awaiting the Asian central bankers meeting in Shanghai later this week which could well come up with major league verbal intervention by the authorities in an attempt to stop the rot.

"This wave of contagion hitting the regional currencies will be a relatively long running affair. The danger is that this is a temporary calm we're seeing," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia.
Supple said the central bankers meeting could yield strong verbal support for the region's currencies but added that he did not expect it to result in actual coordinated intervention.

"There's a broad-based reassessment of risk-reward valuations in the region. Given that genuine funds are leaving as well as speculators, that significantly increases the cost to the real economy of any intervention," he said.
In Malaysia, the ringgit received a boost from Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's displeasure with the recent speculative assault on the currency.
News reports quoted Mahathir, due to return to Malaysia on Tuesday after a two-month absence, as saying there may have been a political agenda behind the recent moves in regional currency markets.
"That's a very strong statement from him. So those funds which were very long (dollars) from below the 2.60 level started to take profit," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.
The ringgit was quoted at 2.6200 to the dollar at 0445 GMT against 2.6270 at its Kuala Lumpur close on Monday.
The Singapore dollar firmed above the 1.46 level against its U.S. counterpart as players turned less bearish after the release of better-than-expected trade data on Monday.
Dealers said wariness of possible central bank resistance was also preventing operators from pushing the Singapore dollar down towards 1.47 to the U.S. dollar.
He said local corporates had sold about $100 million from the 1.4635 level, but the U.S. dollar was likely to meet fresh buying interest around 1.4550.
In Indonesia, the rupiah hovered around the 2,600 to the dollar level after an aggressive speculative attack on Monday.
"It's a fight to break the 2,600 resistance level for the rupiah. Singapore players are defending the resistance. We are waiting to see who has more bullets," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said.
The rupiah became the latest victim of a speculative attack, plunging about 150 points to a historic 2,665 low against the dollar before staging a marginal recovery on central bank intervention.
Indonesian Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said on Tuesday the attack on the rupiah was not related to fundamentals and the government had no plans to change its monetary policy.

The Thai baht lost ground in domestic markets, where players returned from a long weekend fretting about the impending release of data on financial institutions' non-performing loans. The baht was quoted at 30.880/30.980 to the dollar in the local market versus 30.42/30.47 baht late Friday.
